newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan strive to settle insurance trade row.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan strive to settle insurance trade row.

text.p: Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky heads to Japan on Thursday for a last-ditch effort to resolve a long-running dispute over insurance and avoid an escalation of trade tensions.

Barshefsky, who meets Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka for talks this weekend, told reporters on Wednesday that the disagreement could not be settled if Tokyo failed to meet U.S. concerns about the timing of deregulation of Japan's huge primary life and casualty insurance market.
"Without that there can be no settlement of the insurance dispute," she said.

The dispute has become a major irritant between the two countries, and could escalate into the kind of damaging trade fight with threats of sanctions that has marked U.S.-Japan relations in the past, if the dispute is not settled by a Dec. 15 deadline.
U.S. officials have declined to say what action they would take if the issue was not resolved, but they said they were keeping all options open.
The fight centers on U.S. charges that Japan is planning to renege on a 1994 trade agreement on the deregulation of its $400 billion insurance market.

The United States said that the agreement calls for Tokyo to deregulate the huge primary life and casualty insurance sector, which is dominated by Japanese companies, before unleashinng competition in the tiny specialty insurance market in which foreign companies enjoy a substantial share.
But the Tokyo government has proposed first deregulating the foreign-dominated sector, which Barshefsky said represented only about one third of one percent of the Japanese insurance market.
"That would be the deregulation initiative that Japan wants to pursue," she said. "This deregulation would stand the (1994) insurance agreement on its head."

U.S. officials say Japanese consumers could benefit from more price competition in a less regulated insurance market. Barshefsky said the United States would hold firm on its position on primary sector deregulation.
"We have made it very clear to the Japanese that without primary sector deregulatory initiatives there can be no settlement of the insurance dispute," she said.
"We will work very hard on that issue, but our position is clear and fixed and will not change," she added.

Mitsuzuka told reporters in Tokyo on Wednesday that he was aiming to resolve the dispute in his talks with Barshefsky Friday night and Saturday morning. Barshefsky leaves Tokyo Saturday afternoon for a meeting in Singapore of the World Trade Organization ministers.

"The gap between the two sides remains large and I expect the negotiations to be difficult, but we will both cooperate to see what we can do and aim for a final solution at the next meeting," Mitsuzuka said. "We will urge the United States to make a strong commitment towards resolving the issue as well as being flexible."
